scope.notes: Inventory in progress (261 rows). Covers Exalted: The Fair Folk's Chapter Three character-creation overview (separately for noble and common raksha, since the two follow different Attribute/Background baselines), the four base castes (Diplomat/Entertainer/Warrior/Worker) with their Caste Abilities/Grace/Controlling Grace/Associations/Sobriquets, the twelve named noble hybrid castes (ascendant/shadowed caste pairings), the five Graces (Cup/Ring/Staff/Sword/Heart) with full dot tables plus their general forging rules, the Bedlam mechanic (this splat's Limit-Trait analog) including all four Virtue-specific Curses and their Lures, the five new Fair Folk Backgrounds (Birth, Freehold, Gossamer, Retinue, Style), the altered Backgrounds (Artifact, Familiar, Manse, Backing/Contacts/Influence) and the excluded ones (Followers, Resources), a set of core signature mechanics (innate Wyld-damage immunity, Craft (Glamour), Wyld stunts/bonuses, Gossamer-and-Glamour Charm fuel, Mutation, Shaping Actions/Reality Shaping, Shaping Combat basics, Oaths, Cold-Wrought Iron), all five of Chapter Five's per-Grace Charm trees in full (Heart/Nirguna 14 rows, Staff/Nirvikalpa 12 rows, Cup/Dharma 48 rows, Ring/Nirvishesha 78 rows, Sword/Nishkriya 42 rows -- pp. 155-205/PDF 156-206 combined), and now the universal, non-Grace-gated Assumption-type Charm tree in full (shinma Nirakara, 'the Mask'; 21 Charm rows, pp. 149-155/PDF 150-156), the Charms every raksha uses to take shape and exist within Creation at all, with no minimum Grace requirement of their own: two independent gateway roots (Assumption of Elemental Shape, consolidated across its five Air/Earth/Fire/Water/Wood variants like Bastion of the Self, and Assumption of Cerements and Bone for the Underworld) feeding a line of region-tainting Charms (Assumption of the Person's/Land's/City's Heart, Living Kingdom, Wyld-Tainted Land) and the permanent Mad God Mien (which resolves a forward reference from the Ring Grace tree's Extinction of Desire), plus two further sub-trees: Elemental Influence (Sovereign Elemental Shape, Element-Weaving Style, Elemental Invocation; World-Angering Elemental Mastery, Teeth of the World; Elemental Transformation and Mercurial Shape) and Emotional Influence, explicitly framed in the book as a worked example of a personalized non-elemental Assumption-type Charm tree (Assumption of Dreams and Passion, Elegant Muse Attitude, Emotion-Weaving Style, Emotional Invocation, Unwanted Obsession Provocation Technique, Essence-Disrobing Passion). One naming slip was flagged: Assumption of the Wyld-Tainted Land's own text says it 'functions as Assumption of the Kingdom's Heart,' a Charm name that does not exist anywhere in the book; its stated Prerequisite Charms line and tree diagram both confirm it actually branches off Assumption of the City's Heart. A seventh pass then added the 'Vexing' rules and 'Questing' sidebar (2 rows, pp. 147-148/PDF 148-149, Sword-shaping-combat-adjacent material immediately preceding the Assumption-type Charm tree): the general Vexing mechanic (seizing possessions/waypoints/behemoth-essence from a loser of a Sword-shaping contest, plus the Willpower + Essence resistance roll for Creation-born victims without a Sword Grace) and the Questing sidebar (raksha who deliberately provoke unshaped god-monsters into shaping contests to win artifacts/spells/servants). An eighth pass then completed all of Chapter Five's remaining material (26 rows, pp. 205-211/PDF 206-212): Glamour Sorcery (the raksha's Artifact-Background-purchased spell system -- five Circle tiers, Waking/Dreaming/Desire/Samadhi/Shinma, plus its framework and countermagic sidebar), Wyld Artifacts (the Ring-forged-treasure category plus three named examples -- Resonant Chorus Bow, Hundred Color Shaping Lens, Artifact Waypoint), Adjurations (the world-shaping-oath category plus its 'How Inconvenient' framing sidebar and five named oath tiers -- Samhara/Sthiti/Anugraha/Tirobhava/Srishti, aspected respectively to Sword/Ring/Cup/Staff/Heart), Behemoths (the Sword-aspected monstrous-companion-artifact category plus Behemoth Powers, three named tiers -- Fey Beast, Daikaiju, Deep Wyld Horror -- and the unique, gm-only legendary example Ishiika, once tamed by the lost Prince Balor), and the apparent sixth shinma Nirupadhika, the Way (determined to be real, rules-complete, narrowly-scoped player-facing content -- two Charms, Forging the Way Grace and Perfect Reckoning Technique -- rather than either a standard sixth Grace or pure GM lore; see rulesNotes for the full determination). This pass also corrected a one-page offset in this file's own prior page estimates for Behemoths and Nirupadhika, found via direct visual confirmation against the rendered page images (see rulesNotes). With this pass, Chapter Five: Raksha Magic is now fully inventoried end to end (261 rows total). Still needed: Chapter One's Rakshastan geography/setting material, Chapter Two's broader raksha lore, Chapter Six's Mountain Folk (a separate playable-adjacent race), and Merits/Flaws specific to Fair Folk (not yet found anywhere in the book).

sources.role: Primary Fair Folk (raksha) rules, character creation, Graces, Backgrounds, shaping magic, and setting material

rulesNotes: This PDF has a real, selectable text layer (confirmed via direct PyMuPDF text extraction on multiple sample pages); it is not image-only like the Lunar/Abyssal source PDFs. Text was extracted directly and cross-checked by visually rendering and reading a sample of pages (character-creation summary tables, Grace dot tables, Background dot tables, the Noble Castes pages, and the Storyteller-only 'unshaped' Charm-suggestion sidebar) with the same render-pdf-pages.py + Read-tool workflow used for image-based books, since dot-rating tables and sidebar boxes are exactly the layout that can scramble during plain text extraction. No scrambling was found in the sampled pages; the extracted text order matched the visual layout in every spot-checked case.

Printed page numbers in this book run exactly 1 less than the PDF (physical) page number for the copy used to build this inventory (PDF page = printed page + 1); both are recorded on every citation. This was confirmed both from the Table of Contents (printed page 7, PDF page 8) and from directly reading the printed folio number embedded in the extracted text of dozens of sampled pages.

Fair Folk (raksha) are structurally unlike Solar/Abyssal/Dragon-Blooded/Lunar creation: there are no Attributes-and-Abilities-only Charms, no five Castes shared uniformly by common and noble characters, and no single universal Limit-Trait analog. Common raksha have one feeding Virtue/Grace/caste; noble raksha have two (an 'ascendant' and a 'shadowed' caste), and the ascendant/shadowed pairing across the four base castes produces twelve distinct named noble-caste archetypes (Anarch, Luminary, Panjandrum, Artisan, Courtier, Xia, Eshu, Imperial Raksha, Strategos, Scribe, Ornamental Raksha, Cataphract). Charms are keyed to five Grace Traits (Cup/Ring/Staff/Sword/Heart) rather than to Attributes or Abilities. The Limit-Trait role is filled by Bedlam, which is Virtue-specific rather than universal: each of the four Virtues has its own named Curse (Hubris/Compassion, Namelessness/Conviction, Alienation/Temperance, Meekness-or-Terror/Valor) with its own trigger and recovery condition, plus a mandatory Lure once any Virtue reaches 3+.

'Heart's Blood' does not appear anywhere in this book as Fair Folk terminology; the raksha's core existential Trait is instead the Heart Grace (fixed rating, not freely purchasable), and their wealth/Charm-fuel resource is called Gossamer, not Heart's Blood. No conflation with the Lunar Exalted's unrelated use of similar terms was found or assumed.

Common raksha and noble raksha are covered as two separate character-creation-overview rows in this inventory (fair-folk-creation-overview-common and fair-folk-creation-overview-noble) rather than one combined row, because the book presents them as two materially different baselines (0-dot vs. 3-dot starting Attributes, 0 vs. 10 free Background dots, 1 vs. 3 Favored Abilities, a cheaper Specialty cost for commoners, a cheaper Major Grace cost for nobles) with two separate condensed summary boxes, not one shared creation track with minor caste variation.

Chapter Five's Charm material (pp. 129-213/PDF 130-214, immediately before Chapter Six: The Mountain Folk starts at printed p. 213/PDF 214) is far larger than a single pass can cover: after the general-rules content already inventoried (gossamer/glamour, mutation, shaping actions, shaping combat basics, oaths, cold-wrought iron), it contains a universal, non-Grace-gated Assumption-type Charm tree (the gateway shinma Nirakara, 'the Mask') plus five per-Grace Charm trees, each opened by prose describing its shinma and closed or interleaved with combat-mechanics sections (shaping attack/soak/wound-penalty rules for that Grace) that were already summarized at the mechanical-overview level in shaping-combat-basics. Across three passes, this inventory has now fully covered three of the five: the Heart Grace tree (shinma Nirguna, pp. 155-159/PDF 156-160 -- Name Charms, Bedlam-Influencing Charms [notable for drawing branches from all five Graces rather than just Heart], Dodge Charms, Resistance Charms), the Staff Grace tree (shinma Nirvikalpa, pp. 193-196/PDF 194-197 -- the 10-Charm 'Laughing Monster Style' combat tree plus the separate 2-Charm 'Society-Forging Charms' tree, Oath Gossamer and Eight-Corner Ring Binding), and the Cup Grace tree (shinma Dharma, pp. 159-171/PDF 160-172 -- 48 Charms across Cup Combat Charms [including the named 'Spirit-Twisting Obsession Style' sub-tree], Feeding Charms, Addiction Charms, World-Shaping Charms and Virtue-Shaping Charms). The Cup tree and this pass's continuation into the Ring tree both surfaced several Charms that are explicitly gated on a different Grace than the section they sit in (e.g. Beguilement and Spite-Summoning Malediction, Cup-tree Charms explicitly marked 'Minimum Staff' and 'This is a Staff-shaping Charm'; Undetectable Lie, a Ring Combat Charm with the same pattern) -- the same cross-Grace-crossover pattern already flagged for the Heart tree's Bedlam-Influencing Charms, now confirmed as a recurring structural feature of this Charm material rather than a one-off. This pass completed the Ring Grace tree's first three named sub-sections (shinma Nirvishesha, pp. 171-192/PDF 172-193 -- by far the largest of the five): Ring Combat Charms (16 Charms, pp. 171-175/PDF 172-176, with two independent roots converging at Sorrowful Firmament Resonance), All-Consuming God-Monster Style (6 Charms, pp. 175-178/PDF 176-179, a Stance-type transformation tree granting a purchasable 'God-Monster Body' with a paraphrased sample gift menu, culminating in the self-annihilating capstone Chimera Exultation), Body-Strengthening Charms (5 Charms, pp. 178-180/PDF 179-181, a stacking natural-soak progression plus the standalone Ox-Body Technique) and Creation-Based Crafting (3 Charms, pp. 180-181/PDF 181-182). The large Glamour Charms section (pp. 181-192/PDF 182-193), including the 'Forging the (Grace) Grace' Charms that let raksha grant Grace Traits to Creation-born characters and the Freehold-anchoring Forging the Stronghold/Glory/Fountainhead/Throne Room Charms, and the Sword tree (Nishkriya, pp. 196-203/PDF 197-204) remain for future passes, in that page order.

A short, apparently sixth Grace called 'the Way' (shinma Nirupadhika) surfaces on p. 212 (PDF 213), immediately before Chapter Six begins, with a 'Forging the Way Grace' Charm and a 'Perfect Reckoning Technique' Charm. It postdates and sits outside the five Graces (Cup/Ring/Staff/Sword/Heart) established in Chapter Four's Traits chapter and used throughout this inventory's character-creation and Grace rows; it has not been inventoried or cross-referenced against the existing five-Grace model and needs dedicated review (likely alongside Glamour Sorcery, Wyld Artifacts, Adjurations and Behemoths, which immediately precede it on pp. 205-212/PDF 206-213) before any claims are made about whether it is a real player-facing sixth Grace, an artifact/enchantment category, or setting-specific NPC material.

A fourth pass added the Ring Grace tree's first Glamour Charms tree (14 Charms, pp. 181-185/PDF 182-186), which crafts/summons servants, territory and wealth for a raksha's court. Monstrous Conceit continues the cross-Grace-crossover pattern already noted above: it is gated on both the existing Undetectable Lie (Ring Combat) and the new Glamour Charm, despite sitting in the Glamour Charms section. The 'Greater Arts of Glamour' sub-section (pp. 185-192/PDF 186-193) -- the Forging the (Grace) Grace Charms and Freehold-anchoring Forging the Stronghold/Glory/Fountainhead/Throne Room Charms -- remains for the next pass.

A fifth pass added the Ring Grace tree's 'Greater Arts of Glamour' sub-section (18 Charms, pp. 185-192/PDF 186-193), which finishes the entire Ring Grace tree. Forging the Heart Grace (off Shape-Forged Servant) branches to the four 'Forging the (Grace) Grace' Charms (Cup/Ring/Staff/Sword) and to Forging the Arcane Redoubt (which anchors a Freehold's eternal bonefire and branches to the four parallel Forging the Stronghold/Glory/Fountainhead/Throne Room Charms). All four Grace-granting Charms together feed Gaping Virtue Mouth (-> Iron Nightmare Muzzle, Ecstatic Reproduction Style, and the Staff-shaping crossover Akshata Sexual Methodology). Forging the Heart Grace also feeds the consolidated Great Works of the (Grace) row (four variants packed into one row, matching Bastion of the Self's precedent) -> the consolidated Unshaped (Grace) Transformation row -> the Sword-crossover Behemoth-Forging Meditation and the self-annihilating capstone Extinction of Desire. The same pass then began the fifth and final per-Grace tree, Sword (Nishkriya, the Sword), completing its Sword Combat Charms section in full (27 Charms, pp. 196-202/PDF 197-203): two independent roots (God-Humbling Victory Sword, Host-Summoning Glory of Command) plus a third root (Scattering the Foe) feeding two further lines that converge on capstones Defining the Parameters of Battle and Fearsome Mien, and the named sub-style 'World-Devouring Warlord Style' (9 Charms) culminating in Preemptive Declaration of Victory. One diagram/header naming mismatch was flagged (Waypoint-Sealing Technique, labeled 'Waypoint Sealing Stance' in its tree diagram despite being Type: Reflexive, not Stance-type). Only the Sword Grace tree's separate 'Mutation Charms' section (pp. 202-205/PDF 203-206) remains to finish all five per-Grace Charm trees; it is next for a future pass.

The same fifth pass then completed the Sword Grace tree's 'Mutation Charms' section (15 Charms, pp. 202-205/PDF 203-206) -- a set of individually purchasable Charms of Shape rather than a branching combat tree, nearly all with no Charm prerequisite, save the linear Hundred-Hand Style -> Millipede Mind -> Grace of the Infinite Revolving Spheres / Harmonious Primordial Spirit line (which explicitly stacks with its own prerequisites rather than replacing them). Racing Dragon Speed is flagged as an outlier: unlike every other repurchasable Charm in this Sword-Grace section, its repurchase cap is keyed to the raksha's Compassion rather than her Sword or Valor; this was double-checked against the rendered page image. With this section's completion, **all five of Chapter Five's per-Grace Charm trees (Heart, Staff, Cup, Ring, Sword) are now fully inventoried** (212 rows total). The next largest remaining block of Chapter Five is the universal, non-Grace-gated Assumption-type Charm tree (Nirakara, 'the Mask'; pp. 148-155/PDF 149-156), which several already-inventoried rows reference by name but which has not itself been reviewed.

A sixth pass completed the universal, non-Grace-gated Assumption-type Charm tree in full (shinma Nirakara, 'the Mask'; 21 Charms, pp. 149-155/PDF 150-156) -- the Charms every raksha uses to become a shaped creature capable of existing within Creation, none of which carry a minimum Grace requirement of their own (a raksha's Combo experience cost for one is instead twice its Minimum Essence). Two independent gateway roots were found: Assumption of Elemental Shape (consolidated into one row across its five Air/Earth/Fire/Water/Wood variants, matching the Bastion of the Self precedent) and, for the Underworld specifically, Assumption of Cerements and Bone. From the elemental root, a line of region-tainting Charms runs Assumption of the Person's Heart -> Assumption of the Land's Heart -> Assumption of the City's Heart -> Assumption of a Living Kingdom / Assumption of the Wyld-Tainted Land, capped by the permanent, no-prerequisite Mad God Mien -- this last Charm resolves a forward reference left open by the Ring Grace tree's self-annihilating capstone Extinction of Desire. Two further named sub-trees round out the section: Elemental Influence (Sovereign Elemental Shape -> Element-Weaving Style -> Elemental Invocation, with Sovereign Elemental Shape separately feeding World-Angering Elemental Mastery -> Teeth of the World, and Elemental Transformation -> Mercurial Shape) and Emotional Influence, which the book explicitly presents as a worked example of building a personalized non-elemental Assumption-type Charm tree (Assumption of Dreams and Passion -> Elegant Muse Attitude -> Emotion-Weaving Style -> Emotional Invocation -> Unwanted Obsession Provocation Technique -> Essence-Disrobing Passion). One naming slip was flagged and double-checked against the rendered page image: Assumption of the Wyld-Tainted Land's own text claims to function 'as Assumption of the Kingdom's Heart,' a Charm name that does not exist anywhere in the book; both its stated Prerequisite Charms line and the tree diagram confirm it actually branches off Assumption of the City's Heart, so the reference is treated as a naming slip rather than corrected or reinterpreted. With this tree's completion (233 rows total), the largest remaining blocks of Chapter Five are the short 'Vexing' rules and 'Questing' sidebar (pp. 147-148/PDF 148-149, immediately preceding this tree, not yet inventoried) and Glamour Sorcery / Wyld Artifacts / Adjurations / Behemoths (pp. 205-212/PDF 206-213).

A seventh pass added the 'Vexing' rules and 'Questing' sidebar (2 rows, pp. 147-148/PDF 148-149): Effects of Damage (Sword damage marked against Valor + Sword, loser is vexed once that sum is exceeded), Vexing (seizing possessions/waypoints/Graces up to the loser's Sword Grace, capped at 5 total artifact levels seized, with a raksha's own Heart Grace sacrosanct unless her Sword Grace is broken), Vexing Places (claiming a waypoint via a 3-mote commitment), Vexing the Unshaped (ripping a fresh three-dot behemoth from an unshaped's Sword Grace, or improving an existing one, at most once per story per unshaped), and Vexing Creatures of Creation (a Willpower + Essence resistance roll for Creation-born victims with no Sword Grace, with Exaltation-tier bonus dice) -- all folded into one vexing-mechanic row, plus a separate questing-sidebar row for the boxed Questing rules. The Sword Grace's shaping-weapon stat table (Entanglement, Extras, Hazard, Horror, Monster, Mutant Warleader, Nishkriya Mask, Personal Prowess) on the same page was deliberately not inventoried as its own row, per the same individual-shaping-weapon exclusion already applied to shaping-combat-basics. Resume point for the next pass: Glamour Sorcery / Wyld Artifacts / Adjurations / Behemoths (pp. 205-212/PDF 206-213), then the apparent sixth 'Way' Grace (Nirupadhika, p. 212/PDF 213).

An eighth pass added Glamour Sorcery in full (7 rows, pp. 205-207/PDF 206-208): the framework row (glamour-sorcery-overview, folding in the short 'Spell Abilities' lorekeeper-mechanic subsection) and the 'Glamour Sorcery and Countermagic' sidebar (glamour-sorcery-countermagic), plus the five named Circle tiers as purchasable Artifact-Background options -- Waking Circle Spell (Artifact •), Dreaming Circle Spell (Artifact ••), Desire Circle Spell (Artifact •••), Samadhi Circle Spell (Artifact ••••, restricted to a raksha who owns his own Heart Grace), and Shinma Circle Spell (Artifact •••••). Each tier is built from its own mutation-point budget (10 to 18 points) requiring at least one Assumption-type Charm mutation, with its own invocation cost in motes/gossamer/scenes and its own Cup-shaping-weapon stat defaults; higher tiers (Desire, Samadhi, Shinma) additionally overcome characters who would otherwise be immune to a work of glamour, forcing them to use a stunt or Charm to see through it instead. This resolves a forward reference: the already-inventoried artifact-background-fair-folk row names glamour spells, behemoths, adjurations, and 'the tools of the Ring' as the treasures raksha actually buy with Artifact Background dots, and this pass supplies the mechanical framework and named examples for the first of those four categories.

The same eighth pass added Wyld Artifacts in full (4 rows, pp. 207-208/PDF 208-209): the framework row (wyld-artifacts-overview -- the Ring-shaping self-crafting bonus, and why only a few Wyld artifacts double as Ring-shaping weapons) plus three named examples as purchasable Artifact-Background options -- Resonant Chorus Bow (Artifact •), Hundred Color Shaping Lens (Artifact ••), and Artifact Waypoint (Artifact •••+, an enchanted mobile Ring-shaping weapon built from one or more waypoints).

The same eighth pass added Adjurations in full (7 rows, pp. 208-210/PDF 209-211): the framework row (adjurations-overview -- unbreakable-oath mechanics, the catastrophic-botch consequence of involuntarily breaking one, and the Freehold-wide Throne-Room-sworn-adjuration rule), the 'How Inconvenient Are a Raksha's Oaths?' framing sidebar (adjurations-how-inconvenient-sidebar, disposition reference-only since it sets tone/design intent rather than adding a mechanic), and the five named oath tiers as purchasable Artifact-Background options, each aspected to one of the five core Graces -- Samhara Oath (Artifact •, Sword), Sthiti Oath (Artifact ••, Ring), Anugraha Oath (Artifact •••, Cup), Tirobhava Oath (Artifact ••••, Staff), and Srishti Oath (Artifact •••••, Heart), each with its own mutation-point budget (2 to 6 points, with the Anugraha/Cup and Tirobhava/Staff tiers halving the mutation cost for the swearing raksha, rounding up) and shaping-weapon stat defaults.

The same eighth pass added Behemoths (5 rows, pp. 210-212/PDF 211-213): the framework row (behemoths-overview, folding in the short 'Behemoth Powers' subsection -- a behemoth uses its attuned creature handler's base Traits, excluding Backgrounds and most Merits/Flaws but including Virtues), three named tiers as purchasable Artifact-Background options -- Fey Beast (Artifact • or ••, built around a guaranteed Knife-Hand Dream + Armament of Flesh natural attack), Daikaiju (Artifact •••, heavy natural armor plus 12 free mutation points), and Deep Wyld Horror (Artifact •••• or •••••, the heaviest-armored tier with natural weaponry equivalent to an attuned Magical Material artifact) -- and one unique, story-specific example, Ishiika (Artifact N/A), a legendary scorpion-behemoth once tamed by the lost Prince Balor. Ishiika is deliberately disposition gm-only rather than selectable: unlike the three generic tiers, it is a specific creature tied to one named NPC and explicitly too vast even for its own tamer to wield against Creation, illustrating the top of the power scale rather than offering a build a player follows -- this matches the task's instruction to skip pure Storyteller-facing creature stat blocks while still inventorying the genuinely player-facing Artifact-Background purchase options (the framework and the three generic tiers) that this section actually supplies. This also resolves a forward reference: the already-inventoried great-works-of-the-grace and unshaped-grace-transformation rows both name-check this material by page number without a cross-reference, since no behemoth rows existed yet.

The same eighth pass reviewed the short 'Nirupadhika, the Way' section (p. 211/PDF 212, immediately before Chapter Six begins) and resolved the open question flagged by prior passes about an apparent sixth Grace. DETERMINATION: Nirupadhika is neither a standard sixth playable Grace nor pure GM/setting lore -- the book explicitly introduces it as 'an example of one of the other shinma the raksha might tame' (associated with Awareness, Sail, and Survival), explicitly calls its Charms 'extremely rare,' and gives only two of them (versus 12 to 78 Charms for each of the five real Graces); it is never mentioned anywhere in the character-creation chapters (Three/Four) already inventoried, and no example raksha is shown starting play with a Way Grace. At the same time, its two Charms are fully rules-complete and genuinely usable in play: Forging the Way Grace (nirupadhika-the-way's framework row, plus forging-the-way-grace and perfect-reckoning-technique as selectable Charm rows) lets any raksha who already knows the existing Forging the Heart Grace Charm grant a Way Grace to a consenting creature as an artifact, exactly paralleling the four already-inventoried Forging the (Grace) Grace Charms (Cup/Ring/Staff/Sword) -- this is the first hint in the book that pattern could extend to any shinma a raksha tames, not just the five core Graces. Given this, Nirupadhika was inventoried as real, narrowly-scoped player-facing content (its own framework row plus its two Charms, all with full citations) rather than folded into the five-Grace model used elsewhere in this inventory or excluded outright as GM-only.

This same eighth pass also found and corrected a one-page offset in this file's own prior estimates for the Behemoths and Nirupadhika page ranges. Earlier passes (based on a pre-render skim) had estimated Behemoths at printed pp. 210-212/PDF 211-213 and Nirupadhika at printed p. 212/PDF 213. Direct visual confirmation against the rendered page images -- reading the printed folio number stamped on each page -- showed Behemoths' framework and 'Behemoth Powers' subsection begin on printed p. 210/PDF 211 as estimated, but that Deep Wyld Horror, Ishiika, and the entire Nirupadhika section (including both of its Charms) actually sit on printed p. 211/PDF 212, one page earlier than previously estimated; printed p. 212/PDF 213 is in fact a full-page illustration with no chapter text at all, marking the true end of Chapter Five ahead of Chapter Six: The Mountain Folk. All citations in this pass's new rows use the page numbers confirmed by direct visual reading, not the earlier estimate.
